title: Democrats Take Congress in a Wartime Midterm, Herzog Taps Eisenkot to Replace Netanyahu, and Washington Expands the Iran Blockade to Land Routes
subhead: Voters frustrated by living costs, tariffs, and an eight-month war with Iran handed Democrats control of the US Congress on Tuesday, prompting President Trump to warn Ukraine it needs a new leader while demanding Justice Department probes of impeachment talk at home. Rather than winding down, the Middle East conflict widened by Saturday: US forces disabled a ship in the Gulf of Oman and launched a task force to cut Iranian land corridors, Tehran lifted its 2,000-kilometer missile range cap, Saudi Arabia signed its first defense pact with Damascus, and Israeli President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot 28 days to form a government without Benjamin Netanyahu.

sections.heading: A Wartime Midterm Flips Congress and Reshapes Washington's Foreign Calendar
sections.body:
Tuesday's US midterm elections delivered a clear check on the White House as Democrats won control of Congress, a result analysts at The Hill and AFP attributed to voter fatigue over the eight-month war with Iran, tariff-driven price increases, and high borrowing costs (AP News, The Hill, AFP). Within days of the vote, President Donald Trump took to Truth Social to demand that the Department of Justice investigate Democratic lawmakers who floated impeachment proceedings against Republican cabinet officials, calling the talk 'extortion at the highest level' (The Hill, Al Jazeera). Inside the Democratic caucus, more than one million people signed a petition opposing Hakeem Jeffries for House Speaker and demanding a competitive floor vote (Anadolu Agency).

The electoral calendar immediately altered US diplomacy toward Kyiv. Two days before the vote, Trump publicly stated that Ukraine needs a new leader, even as Russian missiles and drones continued striking Kyiv's bridges and energy infrastructure (AP News, Euronews). Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan spoke by phone with Trump on Saturday to press for diplomatic off-ramps in both the US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, while Britain and France announced a 2,800-troop exercise across 11 nations in Poland to rehearse deploying a postwar stabilization force to Ukraine (Bloomberg HT, Defense News).
sections.whyItMatters: A Democratic majority taking office in January gives European and Middle Eastern capitals a fixed two-month timeline during which the White House still holds unified legislative backing for war funding and sanctions waivers.

sections.heading: From Sea to Land: The Iran Blockade Widens as Tehran Drops Its Missile Range Cap
sections.body:
The week opened with diplomacy on a countdown clock after a Doha draft framework put reopening the Strait of Hormuz on a seven-day timeline and Iran set a two-day pricing ultimatum while a Qatari LNG carrier was struck in the Gulf. By Saturday, coercion had replaced negotiation on both sides. US Central Command (CENTCOM) fired on and disabled a commercial cargo ship attempting to run the naval blockade in the Gulf of Oman, noting that 147 vessels have been redirected to date, and the Pentagon stood up a new task force to interdict Iran's overland supply routes across the region (AP News, CBS News, Al Jazeera).

Tehran answered by announcing it had formally lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit on ballistic missile ranges, while the IRGC claimed two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire near Hormuz after switching off their transponders (AP News, Anadolu Agency). Meanwhile, the USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group pulled into Singapore on Friday on its way to become the third US carrier strike group in the Middle East, and major commodity houses Trafigura, Vitol, Mercuria, and ADNOC lobbied Washington for licenses to put sanctioned oil tankers back into service as freight rates soared (USNI News, OilPrice).

Across the Arabian Peninsula, Saudi Arabia activated civil defense sirens in Dhahran, Abqaiq, Dammam, and Al-Ahsa during Houthi clashes, US energy officials said a damaged Saudi oil pipeline should restart within days, and the Wall Street Journal revealed how commercial shippers routinely email Houthi rebels directly to clear passage through the Red Sea (Times of Israel, EnergyNow, Wall Street Journal).
sections.whyItMatters: Washington's expansion of the blockade to overland corridors and Tehran's removal of its 2,000-kilometer missile cap move the conflict beyond the Gulf waterway into a wider contest over land transit and medium-range strike reach.

sections.heading: Herzog Hands the Mandate to Eisenkot as Riyadh Signs a Defense Pact With Damascus
sections.body:
Ten days after Israel's inconclusive October 27 election left Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc short of a majority, President Isaac Herzog announced on Saturday night that he is tasking former IDF chief of staff and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the next government (Reuters, AP News, CNA). Backed by recommendations from 67 of the Knesset's 120 members and potential external support from Arab parties holding 19 seats, Eisenkot now has 28 days — plus a possible 14-day extension — to build what he called a 'national emergency government' (Washington Post, Dünya, Anadolu Agency). Analysts told Breaking Defense that any post-midterm US congressional conditions on military aid would directly affect Israeli acquisition timelines for F-15 and F-35 jets and Apache helicopters.

The regional map around Israel shifted just as quickly. Saudi Arabia signed its first formal defense cooperation agreement with Syria's new leadership in Damascus — covering military training, intelligence sharing, and rebuilding Syria's armed forces — days after the Turkish parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee advanced the trilateral Makkah Defense Pact (Breaking Defense, Anadolu Agency). In the South Caucasus, Armenian Security Council Secretary Alen Simonyan declared that Russia's military base would not protect Armenia and called for rapid normalization with Turkey as Yerevan began design work on the US-backed TRIPP transit corridor and President Erdoğan traveled to Azerbaijan for Victory Day (Star, OilPrice, Milliyet).
sections.whyItMatters: An Eisenkot-led coalition in Jerusalem and a Saudi-Syrian defense pact in Damascus would simultaneously alter the two central alignments that have defined Levant security since 2023.

sections.heading: AI's $1.25T Peak Meets Espionage, a $6.3B Crypto Theft, and Power Grid Reality
sections.body:
The technology sector experienced both record capital concentration and severe security shocks this week. OpenAI closed an $11 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation, even as AI infrastructure builders hit local political resistance across the United States that forced Crusoe to sell a troubled Wyoming data center project to Google while China converted potato farms in Inner Mongolia into sprawling AI compute hubs (TechCrunch, Wall Street Journal, CNA). On the supply side, OilPrice warned that America's nuclear power revival faces a domestic uranium fuel bottleneck and $50 billion in unplaced nuclear waste, while European gas traded at 114 euros per megawatt-hour with winter storage at 75 percent.

Security breaches struck the industry's core players. The Financial Times reported that US intelligence believes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was targeted via a romantic relationship with a Megaspeed executive recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, while $11.4 million in Nvidia hardware vanished in transit between Oakland and Texas (Financial Times, TechCrunch, Ars Technica). In digital assets, North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance — prompting the exchange's CFO to depart days later — and blockchain tracker Chainalysis suffered an AI-assisted multifront breach that exposed customer credentials and tokens (TechCrunch, Ars Technica).
sections.whyItMatters: Capital is still pouring into frontier AI at trillion-dollar valuations, but physical power bottlenecks, state-backed cyber heists, and supply-chain espionage are imposing hard operational costs on the buildout.

sections.heading: Internal Shocks From Kraków to Asunción and a Knife-Edge Vote in Wellington
sections.body:
Domestic political and security shocks hit four continents over the week. In Poland, a gunman influenced by far-right ideology opened fire from a car in Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday, killing six people — including a British citizen — and injuring 15, before police found three more bodies at his home; Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the shooting an act of terrorism and President Karol Nawrocki declared two days of national mourning (BBC, Al Jazeera, The Independent). Meanwhile, 146,000 protesters marched in France as prosecutors investigated foreign state links to aviation bomb hoaxes, and Spain's Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency after 3,300 migrant boat arrivals in a week (NTV, DW, Al Jazeera).

In South America, a systemic banking freeze in Paraguay toppled President Santiago Peña and led a judge on Saturday to order his preventive detention on criminal charges, while a drone attack on a military base in Colombia killed three soldiers during a week of joint US-Colombia military exercises (BBC, Anadolu Agency, AP News). In the Pacific, New Zealand's general election ended on a knife-edge with the center-right holding a provisional one-seat margin ahead of weeks of special ballot counting (The Guardian, Times of Israel).
sections.whyItMatters: From a banking collapse that jailed a Paraguayan president within days to a hung parliament in New Zealand and terror in Kraków, domestic shocks are consuming government bandwidth while major interstate wars grind on.

bottomLine: This week the political and military clocks of the eight-month Iran war diverged. American voters handed Congress to the Democrats on Tuesday in a rebuke shaped by wartime inflation, yet by Saturday the Pentagon had expanded the Iran blockade to overland supply corridors and disabled a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, while Tehran lifted its 2,000-kilometer ballistic missile range cap and reported two tankers hit by mines near Hormuz. At the same time, Israeli President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot 28 days and a 67-seat mandate to replace Benjamin Netanyahu, Saudi Arabia signed its first defense agreement with Syria's new leadership, and Armenia publicly broke with Russian security guarantees in favor of normalizing ties with Turkey. Watch four developments next week: whether Eisenkot secures formal coalition terms with Israel's opposition parties, whether the damaged Saudi oil pipeline returns to service on schedule, how markets digest the Antalya COP31 energy agenda, and whether Kyiv's upcoming talks with Washington and Moscow gain traction before the new US Congress convenes.
sources: Reuters, AP News, AFP, Al Jazeera, BBC, The Guardian, New York Times, Washington Post, Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, Bloomberg, CNA, SCMP, DW, Euronews, CBS News, NBC News, The Hill, The Independent, Times of Israel, Breaking Defense, Defense News, USNI News, The War Zone, OilPrice, EnergyNow, TechCrunch, Ars Technica, UKMTO, Anadolu Agency, Dünya, Ekonomim, Bloomberg HT, Habertürk, NTV, Milliyet, Star
